title: Units of data storage
starter: A light switch has two positions. Explain how you could send a message to a friend using only that switch.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Why binary?
facts: Computers are built from transistors, which are switches: on or off.
Two states map perfectly onto 1 and 0.
Everything, from numbers to images and sound, is stored as binary.
stations.challenge: Why is data stored in binary?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Computers are built from transistors, which are switches: on or off.
Also credit: Two states map perfectly onto 1 and 0.

questions.a: Their circuits have two states, on and off, which represent 1 and 0

questions.q: Which of these is stored in binary inside a computer?
questions.a: All of them: numbers, text, images and sound

stations.name: Bits, nibbles and bytes
facts: A bit is a single 1 or 0.
A nibble is 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits.
One byte can store one character, or a number from 0 to 255.
stations.challenge: Show how the number 5 is stored in a nibble.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A bit is a single 1 or 0.
Also credit: A nibble is 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits.

questions.q: How many bits are in a byte?
Show the number 5 in binary. Use the last four bits, as a nibble.

stations.name: Kilo, mega, giga
facts: 1 gigabyte (GB) = 1,000 MB. 1 terabyte (TB) = 1,000 GB. 1 petabyte (PB) = 1,000 TB.
stations.challenge: Write the units in order and show each as a power of ten.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: 1 kilobyte (kB) = 1,000 bytes. 1 megabyte (MB) = 1,000 kB.
Also credit: 1 gigabyte (GB) = 1,000 MB. 1 terabyte (TB) = 1,000 GB. 1 petabyte (PB) = 1,000 TB.

questions.q: Put these units in order, smallest first.
questions.a: Bit → Nibble → Byte → Kilobyte → Megabyte → Gigabyte → Terabyte → Petabyte

questions.q: How many megabytes are in a gigabyte?

stations.name: Converting units
facts: Going up a unit: divide by 1,000. Going down: multiply by 1,000.
Bits to bytes: divide by 8. Bytes to bits: multiply by 8.
Watch the capital B: KB is kilobytes, Kb is kilobits.
stations.challenge: Convert 4,500 MB into gigabytes, and 3 GB into megabytes.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Going up a unit: divide by 1,000. Going down: multiply by 1,000.
Also credit: Bits to bytes: divide by 8. Bytes to bits: multiply by 8.

questions.q: How many bytes are in 2 kB?
A file is 6,000 MB. How big is it in gigabytes?
What does a lowercase b mean, as in 34 Kb?
questions.a: Kilobits, used for data transmission speeds

stations.name: Storing a number
facts: 1 bit stores a Boolean: true or false, 1 or 0.
A nibble stores 0 to 15: enough for a single digit on an LCD display.
A byte stores 0 to 255: enough for one character, such as A = 65.
stations.challenge: Show how 65 is stored in 8 bits.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: 1 bit stores a Boolean: true or false, 1 or 0.
Also credit: A nibble stores 0 to 15: enough for a single digit on an LCD display.

questions.q: Show the number 65 in 8-bit binary. This is the code for the letter A.
What is the largest number a byte can store?

stations.name: How big is a petabyte?
facts: It would hold roughly 250,000 films, or 200 million photos.
Data centres now measure their storage in petabytes and exabytes.
stations.challenge: How many 8 GB memory sticks would it take to hold 1 PB?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: 1 PB is a million gigabytes.
Also credit: It would hold roughly 250,000 films, or 200 million photos.

questions.q: How many gigabytes are in a petabyte?
Roughly how many 8 GB memory sticks would hold 1 TB?

final.name: Final challenge: unit conversions

questions.q: Sort these into the correct unit.
questions.a: 1,000 bytes = Kilobyte; 1,000,000 bytes = Megabyte; 1,000 kB = Megabyte; 1,000 MB = Gigabyte; 10⁹ bytes = Gigabyte; A typical short photo file = Megabyte

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: State how many bits there are in a byte.
points: A nibble is 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits.
One byte can store one character, or a number from 0 to 255.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
